The system uses a low-power (approx. 10 mW) wideband linear-FM radar with swept bandwidth exceeding 3 GHz.
Range resolution achieved is better than 10 cm, with examples showing 5-10 cm resolution.
Center frequencies of 7.5, 10, and 15 GHz are used in different system configurations.
Two homodyne receivers are employed: one processes a delayed reference signal, the other processes the received echo.
FFT processing with 1024 points is used for spectral analysis and range profile generation.
Range sidelobes are reduced from 13 dB to approximately 40 dB below the main peak by applying tapered window functions.
Targets measured include metal spheres (1 inch diameter), cylindrical rods, square ducts, flat plates with radar absorbing material, scale aircraft models, and a BQM-34S drone.
Two-dimensional RCS images are generated by combining range profiles with Doppler processing from target rotation increments of about 0.1 degrees.
Calibration is performed using metal spheres with known RCS to correct system frequency-dependent effects.
The fundamental range resolution formula is AR = c/(2B), where c is the speed of light and B is bandwidth.
Frequency responses of targets show expected variations including lobes and interference patterns consistent with target geometry.
The system produces real-time CRT displays of range profiles with processing times under 10 ms for FFT and about 15 s for annotated plots.
Measurements are conducted in tapered anechoic chambers approximately 8 m wide, 5 m high, and 22 m long.
Spurious reflections from the chamber and support structures cause low-level background responses that are minimized by background subtraction.
Two-dimensional images reveal discrete scattering centers corresponding to physical features such as wingtip pods, tail structures, and edges on scale aircraft models.
The system uses a feedback loop to linearize the frequency sweep of the RF source.
Range profiles are obtained by Fourier transforming the homodyne receiver output signal, which is proportional to the target range.
Cross-range resolution is obtained by Doppler processing of signals reflected from rotating targets.
The system can generate RCS data as a function of frequency, range, cross range, and aspect angle from a single measurement setup.
The measurement system enables diagnostic analysis of complex targets by isolating individual scattering sources.
